title: Reconstructing Balenciaga: From 1995 Archives To Clo
description:
CSDMM-UPM is bringing historical fashion into the digital age. This video follows the meticulous reconstruction of original Balenciaga patterns from 1995 using CLO, revealing how technology can illuminate the construction logic of a master. Guillermo García‑Badell and María Luisa Calvo from Centro Superior de Diseño de Moda de Madrid (CSDMM) guide us through the process of recovering and interpreting archival material to understand Balenciaga’s design methodology. The project demonstrates how digital tools are becoming essential for historical research, academic innovation, and the preservation of fashion heritage.

🇪🇸 Reconstruyendo a Balenciaga: de los archivos de 1995 a CLO

El CSDMM-UPM traslada la historia de la moda a la vanguardia digital. Este vídeo documenta la minuciosa reconstrucción de los patrones originales de Balenciaga de 1995 mediante CLO, y revela cómo la tecnología es capaz de arrojar luz sobre la magistral lógica constructiva del diseñador. De la mano de Guillermo García‑Badell y María Luisa Calvo, nos adentramos en el delicado proceso de rescate e interpretación del material de archivo para comprender en profundidad la metodología de diseño de Balenciaga. Este proyecto evidencia cómo las herramientas digitales se han consolidado como un pilar imprescindible para la investigación histórica, la innovación académica y la preservación del patrimonio en el mundo de la moda.

transcript: This is definitely transforming the way in which we can disseminate and in which we can investigate pieces of clothing. As a university, in the end, the mission is always triple. It is to educate, it is to investigate and it is to transfer the knowledge created to society. We continue to be committed to innovation, to research, and those patterns of that time are now taking place in 3D recreations, in digitalizations of another level, which continue to make us leaders in the sector. When we started with the research, the first step was to locate all the material that we had in the Superior Center for Fashion Design related to the 1995 exhibition. We realized that we also kept a series of original patterns, our main objective was to reconstruct those prototypes that had been exhibited in 1995. The most striking thing, I would say, is that deeply abstract character of the patterns, which is something very characteristic of Cristóbal Valenciaga. I mean abstract in that they are super beautiful, precious shapes, but it is very difficult to identify at first glance where a skirt is, where a armchair is, or where a skirt is. To have a starting point, I tried to find in each of the patterns that we had some kind of line, a contour line, for example, that could give me an idea of an approximate reference of the size of the body. A clear example is in the dress. In the dress the hip line was very well identified and I could see that it was a hip line of 90 centimeters. Therefore, clearly, we had to work with an avatar of a very small size. Well, Claw was absolutely indispensable in this process. It allowed us to test different hypotheses about the construction of the garments in an efficient way. We were able to save a lot of time and also a lot of materials. Well, the fact that, as I said, we did not know both the measurement and the general shape of the body, which has to go under each of these trident, made the avatar editor of Claw undoubtedly the star tool. Right? As a pattern maker, I am used to creating my pattern, creating my tual, and then adjusting that tual on a body. However, here I could not do that because I could not modify the geometry of the original pattern. So, to achieve a good garment adjustment, what I had to do was to modify both the measurements and the avatar posture, instead of touching the pattern. This is something that, if we had wanted to carry it out physically, it would have been very, very difficult. Well, at all times, when it came to an investigation, I tried not to alter the original geometry of the pattern, unless it was strictly necessary. There were, for example, pattern corners that had to be, that had to be exactly 90 degrees, because they were not exactly 90 degrees, right? And this is probably due to the instability of a fabric. So, those small deviations, they were corrected to, for example, avoid having peaks appearing on the bottom of a garment and things like that. These virtual reconstructions have allowed us to reveal the appearance of the three missing tuals. And we have been able to link these patterns with specific designs that are preserved in the Museo Cristóbal Valenciaga in Guetaria. Well, I think this project is a good example of the value of digital reconstruction in research, right? But it also seems to me key, this value that it has as a didactic tool and as a tool for dissemination, after all. I would like to do many things with Clo.
markdown_content: ## Research Mission and Digital Reconstruction Goals This section frames the project’s academic mission (educate, investigate, and transfer knowledge) and explains how 3D and digital methods are being used to advance research and dissemination in fashion. The speaker emphasizes that, as a university, the mission is triple: **education**, **research**, and **knowledge transfer to society**. They highlight ongoing commitment to **innovation** and **research**, noting that patterns from earlier periods are now being recreated through **3D recreations** and higher-level **digitalizations**, positioning the team as leaders in the sector. The focus of the work described is reconstructing garment prototypes originally exhibited in **1995**. The speaker states that the first research step was to locate all relevant materials held in the **Superior Center for Fashion Design** related to the 1995 exhibition. They also mention that a series of **original patterns** were preserved, and the main objective was to **reconstruct the prototypes** that had been exhibited. A key theme is the **deeply abstract character** of **Cristóbal Balenciaga** (spelled as “Cristóbal Valenciaga” in the transcript). The patterns are described as visually beautiful and precious, but difficult to interpret at first glance—e.g., distinguishing where a **skirt** ends and another form begins, or where an object like an **armchair** shape is represented in the pattern. This abstractness creates the need for careful measurement references and computational tools to make the reconstructions physically meaningful. ## Locating 1995 Patterns and Establishing Body Reference Lines This section explains how the team uses contours/lines in the original patterns to estimate body proportions when reconstructing garments from abstract pattern geometry. To create a starting point, the speaker describes searching within each preserved pattern for a **line** or **contour line** that could estimate the **approximate body size reference**. The example given is a **dress**: the **hip line** is identified clearly, and it corresponds to a measured value of **90 centimeters**. Because the hip line reference is known (90 cm), the reconstruction process requires working with an **avatar of a very small size**. The speaker indicates that the team did not know both the **exact measurements** and the **general body shape** that would correspond to each pattern, so the avatar workflow becomes essential for testing hypotheses about garment construction and fit. ## Why Claw Was Essential for Testing Construction Hypotheses This section describes the role of **Claw** in virtual garment reconstruction, including hypothesis testing and reducing time and material waste. The speaker states that **Claw** was “absolutely indispensable” in the process. It enabled the team to **test different hypotheses** about **garment construction** efficiently. They emphasize practical benefits: **saving time** and **saving materials**. The transcript also clarifies the tool’s necessity due to missing information about the final body measurements and shape. The speaker notes that because they did not know the body’s measurements and general geometry, the **avatar editor of Claw** became the “star tool.” ## Pattern Maker Workflow Change: Modifying Avatar Rather Than Original Geometry This section explains the constraint that the original pattern geometry could not be altered, so the fit was achieved by adjusting avatar measurements and posture in Claw. The speaker contrasts their usual patternmaking workflow with the project’s constraints. Normally, as a **pattern maker**, they would create a pattern (the transcript includes “tual,” likely referring to a physical toile/mockup concept) and then adjust it on a body. In this virtual reconstruction, that approach was not possible because they **could not modify the geometry of the original pattern**. To achieve a good garment adjustment, the required changes were: - **Modify both the measurements** of the avatar - **Modify the avatar posture** - **Do not touch** the original pattern geometry The speaker notes that attempting this physically would have been **very, very difficult**, reinforcing why the digital pipeline was necessary. They also state a guiding principle during investigation: they tried **not to alter the original geometry** of the pattern unless it was strictly necessary. ## Correcting Geometric Deviations and Fabric-Induced Instability This section covers how exact geometric requirements (e.g., 90-degree corners) were enforced virtually, and how deviations were corrected to prevent garment defects. The speaker mentions that some pattern corners needed to be **exactly 90 degrees**. In the preserved patterns, certain corners were **not** at 90 degrees, which they attribute to **fabric instability** (i.e., distortions introduced by how fabric behaved or was handled historically). Small deviations were corrected to avoid issues such as **peaks appearing on the bottom of a garment**. This indicates the team’s careful balance: preserve original pattern geometry whenever possible, but apply targeted corrections when necessary to ensure realistic garment outcomes. ## Linking Virtual Reconstructions to Museo Cristóbal Valenciaga Designs This section describes what the virtual reconstruction revealed (missing toiles) and how the reconstructed patterns were matched to preserved designs in the museum collection. The speaker states that these **virtual reconstructions** allowed them to **reveal the appearance of the three missing “tuals.”** They also describe linking the reconstructed patterns with **specific designs preserved** in the **Museo Cristóbal Valenciaga** in **Guetaria** (transcript spelling: “Guetaria”). Finally, the speaker frames the project as a demonstration of the value of **digital reconstruction** in research, while also emphasizing its importance as a **didactic tool** and for **dissemination**—not only for academic investigation but for broader educational access to the work.
